To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the effects of anthropogenic pressures are not only direct but also indirect and (ii) the indirect effects can be more significant than the direct effects.
land use effects on stream ecological status are mediated by both direct and indirect effects of hydromorphism.

(i) land uses have a strong indirect effect on stream ecological status, (ii) the effects of hydromorphic alterations on stream ecological status are partly indirect and (iii) hydromorphic alteration effects on macroinvertebrates are mainly exerted via substrate characteristics and nutrient-organic matter concentrations at site scale.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new modelling approaches to better describe the relationships between anthropogenic pressures, stream hydromorphism and ecological status.
the indirect impacts of land use on stream invertebrate assemblage composition, and how these indirect effects are transmitted through the stream continuum.
the indirect effects of multiple anthropogenic stressors on stream ecological status at different scales, with the aim to provide better information for water managers and policy makers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the consideration of indirect effects of land-use changes and hydromorphic alterations on stream ecological status has led to a better understanding of the role of hydormorphology in the determination of the ecological quality of running water ecosystems.

land use and hydomorphological alterations have a major indirect impact on macroinvertebrates assemblages, through the modification of the substrate mosaic structure, and that the hierarchy between the impacts of anthropogenic pressure types on stream ecological status has to be reconsidered.

land use and hydomorphological alterations have a strong impact on stream invertebrate assemblage structure through their indirect effects on substrate characteristics and on the concentrations in nutrients and organic matter, and that the hierarchy and strength of the impacts of anthropogenic pressure types on stream ecological status should be reconsidered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the indirect effects of multiple anthropogenic pressures on benthic macroinvertebrate communities have to be taken into account to correctly assess stream ecological status.
the indirect effects of multiple anthropogenic pressures have to be included in the evaluation of the ecological status of streams.
land use and hydomorphology are the most important pressures impacting stream invertebrate assemblage structure, and thus stream ecological status.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the consideration of the nested scales in a model describing the links between anthropogenic pressure and stream ecological status is essential to understand the role of hydormorphological alterations in this relationship and to better identify the main stressors impacting stream ecological status.

a more comprehensive approach to the analysis of the relationships between anthropogenic pressures, stream hydromorphic and physico-chemical characteristics and macroinvertebrate communities, is required in order to better understand stream ecological status.
the consideration of the spatial scale in the modelling of the relationship between pressures and ecological status is a key step to better understanding of stream ecosystem functioning.
